tier_reason: README #results numbers match exactly (1M: 72.3 vs 71.9 ms; 2M: 157.4 vs 156.3 ms; insert 0.72x, hit 1.69x, miss 1.21x), and benchmark_final_sota.cpp plus the g++ command are public. No CPU model is given, so C. The only comparison is against ankerl::unordered_dense, another third-party library. No std::unordered_map or other incumbent is compared anywhere in the repo.

corrections.caveats: Compares only against ankerl::unordered_dense (a third-party library), never against std::unordered_map or any other stdlib/incumbent, so it gives no evidence against a default baseline. Total-time win is within noise (0.6% at 1M, 0.7% at 2M). It loses at 100k-500k and is 0.72x on inserts. Single-shot timings with no repetitions. The 1M operation-breakdown table sums (ankerl 160.2 ms vs GS 136.1 ms) do not match the 1M size-table totals (72.3 vs 71.9 ms), which suggests separate noisy runs. The benchmark #includes ankerl_unordered_dense.h, which is not vendored in the repo. INSIGHTS.md and EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md are listed in the README but do not exist in the repo. The table has no deletion and no resizing (fixed capacity) and is SSE2/x86-64 only. The whole repo was created and last committed on 2025-12-23 and credits an AI 'Deep Research' tool. No CPU model stated.

notes: Reject: the only baseline is ankerl::unordered_dense (itself on the known list), which is a third-party library rather than the stdlib/incumbent, and the 'win' is a sub-1% tie on total time. Metadata checks out (MIT, 50 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-12-23).

notes: Real, notable entry (3,217 stars, Apache-2.0, active, last commit 2026-09-10). The record's caveat saying there was no linked raw data or script was wrong: the writeup links the repo, which contains benchmark/bench.cc, the Makefile and CSV results. Tier C unchanged.

tier_reason: arXiv 2502.10831 Tables 1-3 give mean speed-up ratios of 5.49 (sin), 5.52 (cos) and 4.44 (tan) vs inbuilt functions. The paper states g++ -std=c++17 -mavx2 -mfma -O3 -march=native and an AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX. The benchmark code is public at src/benchmark.cpp (seed 2024873, 1000 angles in [-1e6,1e6], 1e5 iterations), and CMakeLists.txt uses the same flags. That meets every A criterion.

corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX (8 cores/16 threads, 3301 MHz max as reported), 2x16 GB (32 GB) DDR 3200 MHz, Windows 10 Home Single Language 64-bit
corrections.caveats: First-party arXiv preprint (cs.MS, Feb 2025), not peer-reviewed. The functions are low-accuracy approximations: the paper reports max abs error 1.5e-3 for sin/cos and 0.27 for tan (max rel error ~3.7e-3 to 6.4e-3), so they are not drop-in replacements for std::sin/cos/tan. The authors' own SIMD Taylor-5 variant was faster (5.83x sin). The benchmark times 1e5 repeated calls on the same single angle through a function pointer (scalar per-call latency, not array throughput). The toolchain is MinGW-w64 g++ on Windows (README: 'MinGW Makefiles'), so the libm under test is the Windows/MinGW CRT, not glibc. The paper calls the baseline 'inbuilt C++ functions' and the code passes ::sin/::cos/::tan. The repo has 7 stars.

notes: Numbers and methodology verified against the PDF and the repo. Tier A stands under the rubric, but the accuracy gap (~3 significant digits) makes this an approximation-vs-exact comparison. The 'throughput' metric label is really per-call latency (metric is not a correctable field).

tier_reason: docs/BENCHMARKS.md unary table at 4096x4096 matches (sin 26.0 vs Eigen3 11.0 GB/s, cos 25.2 vs 11.0, exp 23.0 vs 16.4, log 17.0 vs 13.1; sqrt and tanh slower). The code is public (benchmarks/compare/unary_axiom.cpp, unary_eigen.cpp), but the doc states only 'Darwin 25.3.0 arm64' with no CPU model or compiler, so it is C.

corrections.baseline: Eigen3 element-wise Array ops (A.array().sin()/cos()/exp()/log() on float32 MatrixXf)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the benchmark doc. The top-level CMakeLists.txt adds -O3 -DNDEBUG (+ -mcpu=apple-m1 on Apple arm64) for Release builds with Clang/GCC. The compiler version and the build type actually used are not stated.
corrections.caveats: On macOS, Axiom's float32 sin/cos/exp/log/sqrt dispatch straight to Apple Accelerate vForce (vvsinf/vvcosf/vvexpf/vvlogf in src/backends/cpu/cpu_operations.cpp and vdsp.cpp). The measured win over Eigen3 is therefore Apple Accelerate's, not Axiom's own kernels. A code comment says Accelerate is internally parallelized, while the Eigen3 comparison binary does not link Accelerate. PyTorch beats Axiom on exp, log, sin, cos, sqrt and sigmoid in the same table. The benchmark is first-party and auto-generated (make benchmark, 2026-02-21). The doc's Test Environment gives only 'Darwin 25.3.0 arm64'. 'M4 Pro' appears only in the README matmul headline. The baseline is Eigen3, not std::transform+<cmath>.

notes: Numbers are accurate and tier C is right. The key finding is attribution: on the benchmarked platform the sin/cos/exp/log wins come from calling Apple Accelerate vForce, so the orchestrator may want to treat this as weak or platform-specific evidence.

tier_reason: The README benchmarks FABE13 sincos against system libm and says 'up to 8.4x' on x86 (in text and chart images only). It has an ARM64/NEON table. The benchmark code (fabe13/benchmark_fabe13.c), compilers and flags are public, but no CPU model is given, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'up to 8.4x' faster than libm on x86 AVX2+FMA (Replit Clang 14 and MacBook Pro AppleClang 16), shown only in chart images with no table. The ARM64/NEON table ranges from 1.00x (N=10) through 2.33-2.56x (N=100-10k) and 1.53x (N=100k) to 4.36-4.44x (N=1M-100M) and 5.82x (N=1e9). Max diff vs libm ~1.2e-11.
corrections.caveats: First-party README benchmark only, with no independent reproduction. No CPU model is stated for any platform. The x86 '8.4x' appears only as a headline and chart images. The ARM speedup is 1.0-2.6x below 1M elements. The benchmark seeds rand() with time(NULL), so it is not bit-reproducible. The libm reference loop is also compiled with -Ofast -ffast-math. The MIT LICENSE file lives at fabe13-old/LICENSE (the README points to it), so the GitHub API reports no license. It uses the author's own branding ('Psi-Hyperbasis', 'Lightcap Initiative') and has no third-party citations.

notes: Downgraded for an overstated claim, not for tier. The record's '4.36-5.82x on ARM64 depending on array size' omits the 1.00-2.56x results at small sizes. Metadata verified: 64 stars, last commit 2025-04-20 (stale), MIT text confirmed in fabe13-old/LICENSE.
